title: Nothing to hand over: MFA and passkeys
performance: On their own work and personal accounts, the viewer turns on a second factor where it is offered, picks a passkey when the choice appears, and refuses any sign-in prompt or code request they did not start

audience.assumed_prior: types passwords every day; has met a texted code or a phone prompt at sign-in; has no picture of what travels between their screen and the site
audience.why: the brief's audience is all employees, non-technical; the knowledge sheet has to define factor, MFA and passkey from scratch
audience.motivation: required security awareness viewing; mild fatigue with security chores, real interest in not losing an account
audience.context: desk or phone, often with sound, mixed first languages; the picture must carry the mechanism without the words

strategy.name: contrast_led
strategy.rationale: the knowledge sheet defines each method by how it differs from the last: a password works for anyone (F2), a second factor needs what the thief lacks (F4), a typed code can be relayed (F9), a passkey answer only works for the asking site (F14). The difference IS the content
strategy.signature_move: the same sign-in story turns again with one change, and the viewer sees on the thief's screen whether the attempt goes through or stops, THEN the change is named

misconceptions.belief: once MFA is on, a phishing page cannot get into my account
misconceptions.why_tempting: the code comes to my own phone, so it feels like a lock only I hold
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F9; not_claimed 'MFA stops all phishing'

misconceptions.belief: texted codes can be phished, so they are not worth turning on
misconceptions.why_tempting: the relay run in sec2 shows a code being stolen
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge F11, F6; not_claimed 'texted codes are useless'

misconceptions.belief: an unexpected sign-in prompt is a glitch, and tapping Accept makes it go away
misconceptions.why_tempting: prompts are routine, and repeated ones are annoying

hook.sketch: You type your password, and the site asks for a code from your phone. What did that second step just stop, and what can still get through?

arc.promise: by the end you can tell which sign-ins a thief can borrow, and which leave them nothing to hand over
arc.bridge_from_prior: opens on Maya's sign-in, the one the viewer did this morning

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a stolen password works for anyone and why a second factor stops that replay
sections.carrier: story: Maya's sign-in and the thief's desk side by side; the copied password opens the thief's screen; with a code on Maya's phone the thief's screen stops at 'enter the code'; two plain bars show the risk cut, labelled with who measured it

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a code typed into a fake page can be relayed while a passkey's answer cannot
concepts: fake login page in the middle (F9)
relay while the code is still valid (F9)
passkey: key kept on the device, signs a fresh challenge (F12, F13)
the answer carries the asking page's address (F14)
nothing to type, nothing to pass on (F15)
sections.carrier: split screen: Maya types into a look-alike page while the thief's screen fills with what she types, letter by letter; then the passkey turn: her phone reads the page's address, large, finds it wrong and stays silent

sections.goal: the viewer can apply three rules to their own sign-ins: turn a second factor on, pick a passkey when offered, refuse a prompt they did not start
concepts: any MFA beats none; text weakest, passkey strongest (F11, F16)
the targeted-attack ladder: text code, phone prompt, security keys (F6, F7, F8)
push bombing and unrequested codes (F10, F18)
sections.carrier: three plain bars for the targeted-attack figures, then Maya's phone buzzing with a prompt she did not start, again and again; she denies it and the thief's screen says denied

arc.payoff: Back to the opening sign-in, now readable: the password could be copied, the code relayed, the passkey answer only fits the real site. The viewer refuses a prompt they did not start.

practice_ladder.what: turns one and two narrated end to end: the copied password opens the thief's screen; with a code on Maya's phone it stops
run three is set up (MFA on, a look-alike page) and the viewer predicts the outcome before it plays
an unexpected prompt appears on the opening screen; the viewer decides before the narrator says refuse

slowdown_at: the passkey answer carries the address of the page that asked

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: MFA is on. You type your password and your code into a page that only looks real. Does the thief get in?
recall_moments.answer: yes: the fake page passes both to the real site while the code is still valid (F9)

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: Remember run one: a copied password works from anywhere. A passkey answer is the opposite: it works in one place only.
A prompt you did not start is the relay from run three, asking you to finish it.

transfer_tasks: This week, open the security settings of one work and one personal account and turn on the strongest second factor offered, a passkey if it is there
The next time a sign-in prompt or a code arrives that you did not ask for, refuse it and do not read the code to anyone

persona.voice: the analyst: calm, exact, a little dry
persona.delivery_notes: finding first on each run, then the reason; a beat of silence before each run's outcome; slower on the address stamp; plain and unhurried on the three rules; never alarmed

gagne.attention: hook: the everyday password-then-code moment and its open question
gagne.objective: promise: tell which sign-ins a thief can borrow
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 opens on this morning's sign-in
gagne.present: sec1 to sec3 as four runs of one exchange
gagne.guidance: signature move: same exchange, one change, then name it
gagne.practice: pause_predict after sec1; the unexpected-prompt decision in sec3
gagne.feedback: sec2 reveals the relay and says why the code felt safe
gagne.assess: payoff: the viewer decides on the unexpected prompt before the narrator
gagne.transfer: transfer_tasks: settings this week; refuse what you did not start

merrill.problem_centered: one sign-in, attacked four ways, runs through the whole lesson
merrill.activation: bridge from the viewer's own daily password and code
merrill.demonstration: each run shows the thief's attempt succeeding or bouncing before it is named
merrill.application: predict run three; decide on the unexpected prompt
merrill.integration: transfer tasks on the viewer's own accounts

mayer.coherence: no thief character, no breach stories; only the exchange and what travels on it
mayer.signalling: one slowdown, on the address stamp; one saturated accent on whatever the voice names
mayer.redundancy: screen carries labels and the two figures only; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each label sits on the token or box it names, appearing as it is spoken
mayer.pre_training: sec1 names factor and MFA before the relay runs

arcs.attention: the open question about a step everyone already does
arcs.relevance: their own accounts, work and personal
arcs.confidence: two worked runs before any prediction
arcs.satisfaction: the opening screen becomes readable and the viewer makes the call
